$comment: The trusted hop, as a table. Three runtimes construct this credential — the
Python loopback (mdrag), the wiki's Next.js proxy, and the Trigger.dev
workflows — and each was written against a reading of ADR 0033 rather than
against a shared statement of the cases. Every hop bug so far has been one
runtime disagreeing with another about a row below.
This file is the statement. Each implementation reads it in its own test, so
'the three agree' is checked rather than asserted. Adding a case here fails
every runtime that has not handled it, which is the point.
`incoming` is the inbound request's identity-bearing headers, lowercased.
`service_identity` is whether the middleware resolved this caller as the
internal service (the tokenless internal-secret branch). `expect` is the
outbound headers, with `SECRET` standing for the configured internal secret,
or `error` naming the failure that must be raised rather than sent.

`applies_to` names the runtimes a case constrains. The wiki proxy is the VOUCHING side of the hop -- it holds no caller token to forward -- so the token-precedence rows are not its cases. Recording that beats a silent skip: a reader can tell 'not applicable' from 'not implemented'.
`not_applicable` gives the reason for each omission, so a reader can tell a deliberate divergence from an unimplemented rule. A row omitted with no reason is a row someone excused themselves from.

cases.name: bearer token is forwarded verbatim
cases.why: The normal case. The caller's own credential is the most specific one and carries their entitlement scopes, which the service identity does not.

not_applicable.wiki: The wiki is the vouching side of the hop -- it holds no caller token to forward. Its own /api/v1 proxy passes a caller's token through untouched, which is a different code path from proxyFetch.

cases.name: x-dc-token is forwarded when authorization is absent
cases.why: Cloudflare Access strips Authorization, so this is the only location a CF-fronted caller can use. Forwarding only `authorization` silently dropped their credential and the loopback 401'd — even though the tool had authenticated them correctly one line earlier.

not_applicable.wiki: Same as above: nothing to forward from the vouching side.

cases.name: a token wins over the service identity
cases.why: Precedence, not preference: the token is the more specific credential and carries scopes the service identity cannot.

not_applicable.wiki: Same as above: proxyFetch never holds both, so there is no precedence to settle.

cases.name: the internal hop vouches for the end user by name
cases.why: The hop carries no end-user token by construction — the caller's session was verified upstream. Re-present the service's own secret and name who it is acting for (mdrag#1050). Without this every loopback write from a wiki caller went out with no credential at all and 401'd.

cases.name: the internal hop with no end user still presents the secret
cases.why: A service acting for nobody in particular is a legitimate caller; it simply vouches for no one. Sending the secret without a name is different from sending nothing.

not_applicable.trigger: The workflows require BOTH halves for a vouch and fall through to the token when there is nobody to name. That is deliberate and stricter: their whole purpose is per-user work, so a nameless vouch would silently attribute it to mdrag's default owner, while the token at least names its own. Discovered by this table -- the trigger runtime was written assuming it matched, and it does not.

cases.name: a raw x-user-email cannot mint the secret
cases.why: Minting is gated on the ContextVar the middleware sets inside its VERIFIED internal-secret branch, never on a header. Otherwise any caller could talk us into presenting a secret they never held.

not_applicable.wiki: proxyFetch reads the secret from the environment and takes the vouched user as an argument -- an inbound header reaches neither, so there is no path to close.

cases.name: nothing to forward fails closed
cases.why: Sending a bare request produces a 401 whose message points at the destination rather than at the missing credential, which is a worse afternoon than an explicit refusal.

cases.name: the stripping host is refused as a destination
cases.why: wiki.datacrew.space strips x-internal-secret and x-user-email from every inbound request BY DESIGN and re-injects them only when it vouches. A hop aimed there loses its identity and answers 200, so every user arrives as the same nobody. Diagnosed the hard way in trigger-dev-workflows#36 and guarded by three separate comments before this became a check.

cases.name: the stripping host is refused however it is spelled
cases.why: A check that only matches the exact string is a comment with extra steps.
